slides.title: How to choose a wine at a restaurant
paragraphs: When the waiter asks you 'what wine do you want?', there is no need to panic: there is a simple method.

Use a practical 3-step method: 1) start from the dish (fish, meat, rich or light), 2) state a clear budget (for example 25-35 EUR), 3) ask for a local wine in that range. Real example: you are in Tuscany, eating pici with ragù, budget 30 EUR. You can say: 'Could you suggest a Tuscan red around 30 EUR, preferably smooth?' In 10 seconds you gave all the right information.

slides.title: Red or white?
paragraphs: The most common question: red or white? The answer depends on the food and the context.

Core rule: the more delicate the dish, the lighter the wine should be; the richer the dish, the more structure the wine can have. Sea bass: fresh white (Vermentino). Steak: red with moderate tannin (Chianti Classico). Useful exceptions exist: grilled tuna can handle a light red (Pinot Noir), while a full-bodied oaked white can pair with creamy poultry dishes.

It is preferable with fish

slides.title: Rule plus exceptions

Do not treat 'red with meat, white with fish' as an absolute law: it is a starting point, not a prison. In the quiz you will learn when to follow the rule and when to adapt it intelligently.

slides.title: How much to spend on a bottle
paragraphs: Price isn't everything, but it helps to orient yourself.

In restaurants, the 20-40 EUR range often offers the best quality-price balance. Under 15 EUR you may still find honest options; over 60 EUR you often pay for rarity, vintage, or prestige. Practical tactic: set a maximum budget and ask for two options in that same range, then choose by profile (fresher, softer, bolder).

slides.title: Smart budget
paragraphs: Now you know how to avoid unnecessarily expensive choices.
A higher price does not automatically mean more pleasure in the glass. Your goal is not the most famous label, but the most suitable wine for the dish and the moment.

slides.title: House wine: yes or no?
paragraphs: House wine can be a positive surprise or a safe choice.

House wine is not automatically low quality: in many trattorias it is a reliable local wine designed to match the menu. To choose well, ask two simple questions: which winery is it from, and can I taste it by the glass first? In informal meals, it can be the smartest quality-price choice.

slides.title: When you don't like wine
paragraphs: It can happen: you don't like wine. How to behave?

Separate two cases: 1) personal preference (not your style), 2) technical defect (cork taint, vinegar note, clear oxidation). In case 1, ask politely for an alternative: 'Could we try something less tannic?' In case 2, it is correct to report it immediately: 'I think this bottle may have a defect, could we check it?'

slides.title: How many wines to order
paragraphs: You don't always need a bottle per person.

Practical rule: one 0.75 L bottle is about 5 glasses. For two people, one bottle is often enough for a full meal. If the menu changes a lot (fish then meat), consider starting with glasses and then deciding on a bottle. The goal is to support the meal, not over-order.

lessons.intro: Some wines improve with oxygen in the glass.
lessons.final: Now you know what it means to let a wine breathe.

questions.question: Letting the wine breathe means:
All wines must breathe a lot.
It is mainly used for:

slides.title: When wine must be "breathed"
paragraphs: Some wines improve with oxygen in the glass.

Letting wine breathe means increasing contact with air: in young, tannic reds it can open aromas and soften mouthfeel. Example: Aglianico or Cabernet may improve after 15-30 minutes. Not every wine needs it: many aromatic whites can lose freshness if left open too long.
keyPoints: Letting the wine breathe means
All wines must breathe a lot
It is mainly used for

slides.title: Useful oxygen, not excess
paragraphs: Now you know what it means to let a wine breathe.
Breathing does not mean waiting for hours every time. It means recognizing when a wine needs to open and when it should be enjoyed immediately.

slides.title: How not to make a fool of yourself
paragraphs: Small social rules about wine that avoid embarrassing situations.

The golden rules are simple: do not pretend to know, ask clear questions, smell before judging, taste before commenting. Avoid absolute statements like 'this wine is wrong' if it is only your preference. Saying 'this is not my style' is accurate and mature.

slides.title: Simple elegance
paragraphs: Now you're fool-proof.
In wine, true elegance is not showing off knowledge, but choosing well with ease. One smart question is better than one fake certainty.
